summary:
The New Testament presents this as Paul's last letter. He writes from a Roman prison, likely during Nero's persecution in the mid-60s, expecting to die: "I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time of my departure is at hand" (4:6). It is addressed to Timothy, his closest coworker, and reads like a farewell: requests for his cloak and scrolls, the note that "only Luke is with me" (4:11), names of friends who deserted him, the memory of Timothy's tears when they parted.

At its center is a charge about succession: "the things that you have heard me say among many witnesses, entrust these to faithful men who will be qualified to teach others as well" (2:2) — four generations of handoff in one sentence. Paul expects seasons when people will not tolerate sound teaching, and his prescription is persistence: preach the word, in season and out of season, with the workmanlike patience of his three images for ministry — soldier, athlete, farmer.

Here too is one of the New Testament's key statements about Scripture: "All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness" (3:16), written with Timothy's upbringing in view; he was taught the sacred writings from childhood by his mother Eunice and grandmother Lois. The letter closes with Paul's verdict on his own life: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith" (4:7). Read it as a handover from one generation to the next.
